ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Privatisation of Railways 
*81. SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are thinking of gradual privatisation of the 
Indian Railways due to resource crunch; 
(b) if so, whether any study is being conducted to identify the right 
areas for future privatisation, to meet ever-increasing demand for 
expanding and modernising the railway network as the conventional 
means of raising funds may not suffice; and 
(c) what has been the past experience of the Railways in associating 
private or pubic sector agencies in running services like "Palace on 
Wheels', etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS (KUMARI MAMATA 
BANERJEE): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) No, Sir. 
(b) Does not arise. 
(c) The past experience of Railways in associating private or public 
sector agencies in running services like Palace on Wheels etc. has 
been generally satisfactory.

KUMARI MAMATA BANERJEE: I appreciate that the hon. 
Member is concerned about the financial position of the Railways. Sir, 
it is a fact that the Indian Railways is the second largest railways in the 
world. Though our budget support has been decreased from 87 per cent 
to 17 per cent in the Ninth Five-Year Plan, yet. this year we increased 
the budget outlay from 17 per cent to 35 per cent. Sir, we have so many 
projects on our hands. So. we need at least 33,000 crores of rupees. 
But we should not consider that Indian Railways is only a commercial 
institution; we have social obligations also. There are so many 
socially-desirable projects. Of cour se, ours is a vast country and we 
have potential areas; but. at the sa me time, we have interior areas and 
rural areas where the common people, the poor people, deserve to see 
the Railway line. Sir, the British Railways is a private organization; the 
US Railways is a private organization; the Japan Railways is a private 
organization, but still they get the Government's support because of the 
passengers' interests and safety angle. I am grateful to the hon: Member 
that he raised this question. So, after these incidents also, I say that the 
British Government — though the British Railways is a private 
organization — because of the safety reason, gives financial support 
worth Rs. 21,000 crores; if we count it in Indian currency. The 
Khanna Committee has also recommended to the Government to 
provide Rs. 15.000 crores, in five years, to the Railways. The Railway 
Convention Committee, the Standing Committee and the Consultative 
Committee have also recommended that. Though we have paucity of 
funds, you will be happy to know. Sir, the freight earnings this year 
have crossed the fifty years' record. Our people are trying their level 
best, and so far as passenger earnings  are concerned; it is the highest. 
Thank you. Sir. 
SHRI NARENDRA MOHAN: Sir. in one of the statements, which 
was published in the 'Observer', dated 20th October. 2000, — it was a 
question relating to privatisation — the hon. Minister has stated, instead 
of going for a consummate privatisation, certain thrust sectors have to be 
identified for private sector, where we have the potential and more 
innovative ideas should creep in. May I know from the hon. Minister 
what are those areas where the hon. Minister is thinking of privatising? 
KUMARI MAMATA BANERJEE: Sir, let me first assure the 
House that we are not going for privatisation of the Indian Railways. 
No. 2, as there is paucity of funds, we have decided to make 
commercial utilisation of land and air space. This asset belongs to the 
Railways. It is a great asset for us. That is why we earmarked 24 sites 
for commercial utilisation of land and air space. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [ 24 November, 2000] 
The House will be happy to know that there are some areas which can 
be developed by the private sector, for example Pipavav port. For this, 
private parties and the Indian Railways are giving 50:50. We want to 
connect the Pipavav port and Surenderanagar. Then, under the Special 
Purpose Vehicle Scheme also, the share of the Indian Railways and 
private parties is 50:50. But that is not for privatisation of the Indian 
Railways. We are making commercial utilisation of land and air space. 
We are adopting such innovative ideas. The House will be happy to 
know that till now, Rs. 53 crores have been earmarked for the 
commercial utilisation of land and air space; except the project that we 
are going in for. There are some port projects; there are some 
warehousing projects and other railway projects where the private 
sector, as also the State Government, can come forward. 
DR. M.N. DAS: Hon. Chairman, Sir, I am sure the hon. Minister of 
Railways is well aware of the fact that a large part of the population of 
India does not know what railways is. There are some areas which are 
rich in mineral deposits, but those mineral resources cannot be utilised 
because of lack of communication. When the question comes whether 
the Government has resources to cons truct new railway lines or not, it 
is known to all that the Government does not have the resources to 
invest enough money for constructing new railway lines. If so, when 
the Government is bent upon to open up various public sector units to 
private companies, why should not the Railways be opened up for 
private enterprise. For the information of the hon. Minister, I would 
like to say, when the British wanted to introduce railways in India, they 
were puzzled as to from where they would get the capital. Actually, 
they wanted to export cotton, jute and other raw materials from the 
interiors of India to the seaport. They also wanted to carry their 
products from the seaport to the interiors of India. Besides, they had to 
move they army from one corner of the empire to the other corner, 
that is, from the Hindukush to Burma. For all these reasons they felt 
the need for railways. But there was no money. They did not calculate 
their resources. And the Government of India said, 'we have no money 
to construct railways in India, would the Indian capitalists come 
forward' — at that time, there were not two classes of capitalists and 
industrialists — would the Maharajas, Nizams and Nawabs invest 
money for the construction of railway?' The Maharajas, Nizams and 
Nawabs were so ignorant that they did not even know what railway 
was. So, there was no question of getting money from that side. 
.Ultimately, the British had to invite their capitalists, their 
industrialists, in Britain. They said that 'we would pay

Misappropriation of foreign exchange by IOA 
*82. SHRI ABANI ROY: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS he pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that Indian Olympic Association 
had misappropriated foreign exchange to the tune of crores of rupees in the 
recent Sydney Olympics; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to probe the activities of the 
Association involved in foreign exchange scandal; and 
(c) if so, by when, and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS 
(SUSHREE UMA BHARATI): (a) to (c) A statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Based on information and reports in the media on the issue of 
conversion of money into foreign exchange and transfer thereof during the 
Sydney Olympics, Government asked IOA to furnish complete details 
in the matter. The IOA has since intimated the details in this regard. The 
matter has been referred to the Ministry of Finance for its legal 
opinion. 
SHRI ABANI ROY: Mr. Chairman, Sir. the answer given by the 
Minister and the question put by me has no relation at all. My point is, 
there should be an enquiry. I have mentioned that there. The Minister says 
that she has asked for the legal opinion from the Ministry of Finance. I 
would like to know from the Minister whether her Department is actually 
probing the matter on which I had raised questions—the question of the 
Olympic Association, the question of the foreign exchange scam, the 
question of the behaviour of the officials with the participants. It is a 
country where hundred crores of people are living. But what we have seen

report that the number of officials was more than the participants. About

Suicides due to depression 
* 85. SHRI DINA NATH MISHRA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to slate: 
(a) whether 10 to 20 million people are suffering from mental illness due 
to lack of awareness and proper (real men I and about half of them commit 
suicide, as reported in The Statesman dated 17th October, 2000; 
(b) whether sixty per cent suicides arc due to depression; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to identify sections suffering 
from psychological disorders and provide them proper treatment; 
(d) whether some NGOs are working in this field; and 
(e) if so, what success has been achieved so Tar in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Epidemiological studies have revealed that 1 to 2% 
of the population have major mental disorders and 5 to 10% suffer from 
minor mental disorders. However, it is not true that half of all the people 
suffering from various mental illnesses commit suicide. In fact, the total 
number of suicides reported in the country as per information available with 
the National Crime Records Bureau for the year 1998 is 104713 only. 
Suicides are commonly associated with depressive disorders, and all 
the persons afflicted with mental di sorders may not be suffering from 
depressive disorders. However, th ere is widespread ignorance about 
various aspects of mental disorders and about the fact that appropriate 
treatment is available for mentally ill patients. 
It- is also not true that 60% of suicides are due to depressive disorders. 
Studies on suicides conducted in different centres in India show that a 
variety 
22 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
of psychological, social, economic and personal factors are responsible 
for suicides. Many persons committing suicide may also be suffering 
from long standing painful or untreatable physical conditions. 
The Government has already initiated a pilot programme of providing 
care for persons with mental disorders in selected districts in the country. the 
District Mental Health Programme is currently being implemented in 22 
districts in 20 States and Union Territories. Its aim is to identify persons 
suffering from serious mental disorders and epilepsy and manage them at 
the primary health care centre and district level by trained doctors and with 
the active support of the families and the community in which the patient 
lives. 
A growing number of Non Govern mental Organizations [NGOs] 
have .recently started showing interest in the field of mental health care as 
well as suicide prevention. Some of the prominent NGOs are the Medico 
Pastoral Association in Bangalore. SNEHA — A suicide prevention 
programme in Chennai, Richmond Fellowship India in Bangalore and 
New Delhi, SCARF in Chennai. San jivini in Delhi and Samaritans in 
Calcutta. NGOs work to increase public awareness about mental illnesses, 
decrease stigma related to mental disorders. Provide rehabilitation 
services to mentally ill, provide residential care and facilities for chronic 
mentally ill, run counselling and walk-in services for persons with minor 
mental disorders, crisis intervention service, etc.

91. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that dreaded disease Kala-Azar has returned to the 
Eastern and North-Eastern States, in a big way; 
(b) if so, whether the reasons therefore have been identified; 
(c) whether any result-oriented action programme, to eradicate Kala-Azar, 
has been/is proposed to be initiated; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. CR 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) Kala-Azar is endemic in the States of Bihar and West 
Bengal and sporadic cases are recorded in Uttar Pradesh. There has been a 
steady decrease in number of cases in the endemic States. 
The Kala-Azar Control Programme is in operation as a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme since 1990-91. Government of India is supplying anti-Kala-Azar drugs 
and insecticides to the affected States. Funds are also provided for IEC, training 
and organising campaigns. The state Governments bear the entire operational 
costs for spraying insecticides and are responsible for implementation of the 
programme. 
The programme has resulted in overall decline of 83.5 per cent in incidence 
and 80% in recorded deaths due to Kala-Azar in 1999 as compared to peak 
registration in 1992. To further strengthen the efforts against Kala-Azar. 
Government of India has constituted an Expert Committee to review the 
programme and to suggest a focussed strategy for elimination of the disease.

(b) Steps taken by the Government to protect wildlife in zoos are as follows: 
♦ Government of India has established Central Zoo Authority under the 
Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 with the objective of enforcing standards 
for housing, upkeep and health care of Zoo animals. Central Zoo Rules 
have also been incorporated under Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 
providing standards and norms for the upkeep, housing and health care 
of animals in the zoos.

the country— 
 
(a) To stop establishment of sub-standard zoos in future. 
(b) To close the zoos where the possibility of bringing the status of 
management of zoo animals to the prescribed standards does not 
exist. 
(c) To provide technical and financial assistance to the zoos which 
have potential to improve and come upto the prescribed standards.

financial assistance of Rs. 27.48 crores to various zoos for the 
improvement of animal housing, upkeep, health care facility, 
veterinary care and rescue centres. 
♦ Central Zoo Authority has organised regular courses with Wildlife 
Institute of India, Dehra Dun for capacity building and grading the skills 
of zoo managers, zoo supervisors and zoo veterinarians. They have also 
been sent to small courses to Jersy Wildlife Preservation Trust, U.K. for 
exposure to zoo management in the developed countries.

closed.

(a) whether leprosy, malaria, polio, T.B., cancer, etc. have been

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) No. Sir. 
(b) to (c) In so far as Leprosy is concerned, there has been a decline 
in the prevalence rate of disease which has reduced from 59/10,000 
population in I9M to 5.2/10.000 by March, 2000. The National 
Leprosy Eradication Programme is aiming to reduce the prevalence 
rate to l/l0.000 population for elimination in near future but the 
eradication of leprosy will take many  years. Reasons for the same are 
(1) Many people hide the disease due to the social stigma attached to it 
(2) Past infections result in occu rrence of new cases (3) Incomplete 
treatment of patients (4) Large scale migration of population causing 
difficulties in early diagnosis and completion of treatment (5; Ignorance 
among a large section of people regarding the facts of Leprosy and 
curability with Multi Drug Therapy (MDT). 
The National Ami Malaria Programme (NAMP) aims at keeping 
malaria under control and as a result, the incidence of malaria has been 
contained between 2-3 million case s annually since 1984. Various 
administrative, operational, logistic factors, developmental projects 
leading to mosquitogenic situations, and technical aspects like 
resistance developed by Malaria parasite to an li - materials and vector 
resistance to Insecticides, etc. obstruct the effective control/elimination of 
this disease.

eradication of Polio is being implemented since 1995 in addition to 
routine immunization

been adopted. During 1999-2000. four nation wide rounds of 
Intensified Pulse Polio Immunization Programme (IPPI) were organized

search of unvaccinated children and vacillating them. Two sub-national 
IPPI rounds in 8 high risk Stales of Assam, Bihar, Gujarat. Madhya 
Pradesh. Rajasthan. Orissa. Uliar Pr adesh and West Bengal were also 
undertaken. The strategy for 2000-2001 is to hold 2 sub National 
Immunization days in high risk States and 2 nation wide rounds in all 
the Stales.

decreased from 80 per lakh population in 1972 to 53 per lakh

adopted under the Revised National TB Control programme (RNTCP) 
which is presently covering about 250 million population and ii is 
expected that by 2002 about 500 million population will be brought

years. Under this programme, the cure rale is above 80% as compared

in September, 2000, it was agreed with the con (en (ion of medical 
scientists that (he ban on non-iodised sal( be continued; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that several medical experts wanted the 
ban against non-iodised salt to continue as any move to withdraw (he 
same could be a national disaster; 
 
(c) whether UNICEF has also expressed concern over Government's 
decision to lift ban on consumption on non-iodised salt; 
(d) if so. the details thereof; and 
(e) what steps the Ministry would take to honour the sentiments 
expressed by various organizations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) In the 
meeting convened in September, the Slate Health Ministers expressed 
their views on the central notification issued on 10.5.2000 which 
proposed to remove (he res(ric(ion on sale of iodised salt for direct 
human consumption. 
Medical opinion is divided about whether it is appropriate to make 
consumption of iodised salt compulsory to combat Iodine Deficiency 
Disorders. There are many segments of the population, including 
medical experts, who do not support the use of compulsion in matters 
relating to public health, and who advocate the need to promote 
awareness, availability and accessibility of iodised salt. 
(c) and (d) UNICEF has expressed concern over the lifting of the 
Central notification restricting the sale of non-iodised salt for direct 
human consumption. 
90 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) The restriction on sale of non-iodised salt was finally removed to 
provide for a system that allows adequate flexibility to accommodate 
those who believe that there should be no compulsion in matters 
relating to public health, and that the use of iodised salt to combat IDD 
should ideally be promoted through creation of greater awareness, by 
monitoring the accessibility, availability and affordability of this 
product. 
The need for a statutory compulsi on for sale of iodised salt is 
contingent upon the local social conditions, dietary habits and slate of 
the economy. This aspect is best judged by the State Governments who 
are belter aware of local conditions and who can enforce the ban in 
such areas where the need is percieved. It was felt by the Central 
Government that the decision whether or not to place a ban on sale of 
non-iodised salt, and if yes,, in which areas should be left to the State 
Governments. Consequent upon that the Central Government withdrew 
its notification in this regard. Similar restriction, however, continues to 
be in force in most States/UTs through notifications issued by them 
under the powers available to States in this regard. 
Compulsory iodisation is not th e sole strategy available for 
promoting the use of iodised salt for combating IDD. Creation of 
greater awareness through IEC and increasing availability, 
affordability and accessibility are ke y factors in this regard, and 
Government proposes to focus on th ese aspects to achieve the same 
objective.

The NPE provides for periodical review and apraisal of the implementation

(i) All 6-14 age children in school/EGS centre/bridge course by 2003. (ii)

All 6-14 children complete eight years of schooling by 2010.

education plans prepared in consultation with Panchayati Raj Institutions witl 
form the basis of District Elementary Education Plans. There will be a focus 
on districts having low female literacy among Scheduled Castes and Scheduled 
Tribes. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan will cover the entire country with a special 
focus on educational needs of girls. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. 
The programme of Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan is likely to be operationalised in 
the current Financial Year.

considerable progress has been achieved in universalising elementary 
education. As a result of these efforts more than 70% children in the 6-14 age

sectors.

636. SHRI RAJU PARMAR; 
SHRI BHAGATRAM MANHAR:  
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to refer to answer to 
Starred Question 294, given in the Rajya Sabha on 11 th August, 2000 
and state: 
154

(a) what are the reasons for purchase of locomotives/coaches from abroad 
when these are being manufactured indigenously; and 
(b) what is the price difference between indigenously manufactured 
locomotives/coaches and the ones purchased from German firms? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS (SHRI 
DIGVIJAY SINGH): (a) The locomotives and coaches running on Indian 
Railways are manufactured with technologies imported in 1950s and 1960s. 
These designs have been stretched to their limits and can no longer sustain the 
present day demands of longer and faster trains. In the meanwhile, technology 
has advanced considerably elsewhere in the world to enable cost effective, 
comfortable and safe operations. The purchase of a small quantity of 
locomotives and coaches from abroad alongwith transfer of technology was 
considered essential to enable our Production Units to manufacture 
state-of-the-art locomotives/coaches indigenously with the latest technology. 
(b) No locomotives have been purchased from German firms. However, 24 
coaches are procured from M/s ALSTOM Linke Hoffman Busch, Germany. 
The price of the imported coach vis-a-vis the indigenous version of same type 
is as shown below:

These prices are, however, not readily comparable due to the following 
reasons: 
1. The price of the imported coach in cludes costs of engineering and 
development, amortised over a small batch of 24 coaches. 
2. The imported coaches are of state-of-the-art technology, whereas the 
coaches currently produced indigenously are of much older design and

the new design, will come down eventually as we take up regular

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN  THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE 
AND TECHNOLOGY (SHRI BACHI SINGH RAWAT): (a) and (b)The 
programmes in the area of bio-technology taking note of the advances, 
relating to agriculture and health care system are regularly reviewed by 
high powered expert committees. The Department of Bio-technology 
has a Scientific Advisory Committee with very eminent scientists from 
India; it has a Standing Advisory Committee-Overseas with very 
renowned non-resident Indian scientists from USA and other 
European Countries. There is a Bio-technology Research and 
Promotion Committee under the chairmanship of a an eminent bio-
technologist; there are 17 expert task forces in specific areas e.g. 
Agriculture and Medical Bio-technology. These expert committees 
review the progress of all programmes at least once a year and also 
identify new areas. 
In Agriculture Biotechnology, there have been significant 
achievements. Research on priority crops such as rice, wheat, mustard, 
chickpea/pigeonpea has given promising leads eg.—using tissue 
culture induced variation two mustard varieties "Pusa Jaikishan* and 
"Pusa Bold' have been released and are popular among farmers; also 
transgenic mustard lines showing re sistance to drought and salinity; 
toward hybrid seed production transgenic male sterile lines and fertility 
restorer lines of mustard, and insect resistant transgenics of rice, cabbage 
and tomato have been developed by incorporating Bt genes. A novel 
seed storage protein gene (ArnAl) from Amaranth has been introduced in 
potato in order to improve nutritional quality. Fully regenerating Coker 
310 line of cotton is available, and sysnthesis of modified Cry 1A (c) 
gene is in progress for developing transgenic cotton cultivatrs resistant 
to bollworm. Recently India has joined International Rice Genome 
Sequencing Programme to sequence part of chromosome 11. Apart 
from high-throughout sequencing experience, the project would lead to 
the development of superior rice varieties resistant to pests and diseases. A 
major initiative on biofertilizer and biopesticide development, field trials 
and training of farmers has given rice dividends. The efficacy of 
various biopesticides has been demonstrated in an area of about

immunomodulator developed at the National Institute of Immunology 
were used by NGOs and private pracu ations for Leprosy control. Two 
vaccines for cholera and rotaviral diarrhoea are undergoing clinical trials 
with encouraging results. A National jai Vigyan Science & Technology 
Mission on Development of New generation Vaccines has been 
initiated for six major diseases viz. Cholera, rabies, malaria, 
tuberculosis, Japanese encephalitis and HIV/AI DS. Certain vaccines 
under this programme are in the advance stage of development. A 
major initiative on genetics, ge nomics and functional genomics has 
given a new insight into disease scenario specially for vaccines and 
diagnostics.

Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, 
Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan. Tripura,

houses and property. Arunachal Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh 
and Andhra Pradesh had flash floods. The cumulative rainfall 
during 1.6.2000 to 11.10.2000 was excess only in 12 out of 35 
meteorological sub-divisions in the country but still a number of 
States faced floods. 
As per reports received from the States this year, 
Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Bihar. Gujarat, 
Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, 
Punjab, Sikkim, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal faced flood 
situations of varying magnitude. The loss and damage to life 
and property, as reported by these States cumulatively has 
been 2782 human lives, 92,927 cattle, damage to 27.05 lakh 
houses and inundation of the cropped area of 34.48 lakh 
hectares. 
The flood management is primarily the responsibility of 
the States. The State Governments concerned took necessary 
relief measures like payment of ex-gratia to the next of kin of 
the diseased, evacuation of people in the marooned areas, 
despatch of medical teams, opening of relief camps to provide 
shelter to the affected people, air-dropping of food packets, 
opening of veterinary centres, supply of relief materials to the 
affected population, restoration of damaged roads and power 
lines on priority. 
The Government of India was in constant touch with 
the affected States and rendered necessary help. The Army 
and Air Force assisted the State Governments in relief 
measures like evacuation of people, air-dropping of food 
packets and relief materials. Centre's share of Calamity Relief 
Fund. 
183 

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November, 2000] 
CRF, has been released to the States as per the Scheme. The 
Central Teams were deputed to many flood affected States to 
assess the situation and I had also made aerial survey of the 
flood affected areas of the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, 
West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh. My Ministry coordinated the 
Central efforts with various C entral Ministries/Departments for 
providing relief to the affected people. Foodgrains at the BPL 
rates have been supplied to the State Governments particularly 
to the State of Bihar and West Bengal. Medicines, 
disinfectants, bleaching powder, halogen tablets, etc., were 
also sent to the affected States. 
As you may be aware, 75% of the annual rainfall is 
received during south-west monsoon period, from 1st June to 
30thSeptember, itself resulting in heavy rains and floods in 
many parts of the country, causing damage to life and property 
every year. The flood prone areas are Andhra Pradesh, 
Assam. Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The 
perennial States in regard to regular floods are Assam, North 
Bihar and Eastern parts of Uttar Pradesh. Central Water 
Commission in the Ministry of Water Resources is concerned 
with flood forecasting. India Meteorological Department 
provides necessary support th rough its Flood Meteorological 
Offices. They cater to the requirements of flood forecasting in 
different river catchment areas. FMOs provide Quantitative 
Precipitation Forecast in respect of catchment areas of 
important river to the CWC. Flood forecasting enables 
forewarning about impending flood, to what extent and for how 
long, so that necessary preparatory steps could be taken in 
time. The flood forecasting network consists of 157 stations 
situated in 11 States. 
Flood proofing measures help greatly in the mitigation 
of distress and provide immediate relief to the population in 
flood prone areas. It is essentially a combination of structural 
change and emergency action, not involving any evacuation. 
The techniques adopted consist of providing raised platforms 
for flood shelter for men and cattle and raising the public utility 
installation above flood levels. The progress achieved in flood 
control works as a result of various measures taken is that 
162,000 Km. length of embankments and 32,003 Km. length of 
drainage channel were constructed, 906 towns were protected 
and 4721 villages protected. 
Monitoring  of floods  is also done by remote sensing 
through satellites  which   is  one  of  the  effective  tools  to  
monitor  floods  and  assessment  of flood  damages  in  terms 
of area  inundated,  crop  area  submerged and villages 
marooned.

SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, since independence, only one committee -- the 
one headed by Shri Kelkar 
200 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
-- had been constituted to find out the reasons as well as 
solutions, so far as floods in the Ganges were concerned. After 
that, no committee has been constituted for this purpose. Floods 
in India have become a regular phenomenon every year. One or 
the other part of the country is always affected by floods. Of 
course, Andhra Pradesh is affected very seriously. This year, the 
State of West Bengal has also been affected badly. Several parts 
of India have been affected. I do not want to level any charge 
against this Government. But Government after Government has 
not taken care to constitute any high-powered committee 
consisting of experts to examine the behaviour of the rivers and 
the reasons behind the floods. These have to be examined. 
Modern technologies are available. We have to have a scientific 
approach and a comprehensive plan to assess this situation. 
Whenever there are floods, which are shortlived, the Central 
Government gives assistance. But that is not sufficient. That 
assistance is only for a short period. If a family gets devastated 
by floods, it takes five to ten years to come back to normalcy, 
Sometimes, families are destroyed or ruined for ever. So, we 
have to evolve a long-term policy. This Government has to 
consider the constitution of a high-powered committee to find out 
the reasons as well as solutions to the problem of floods. After 
all, it is not difficult for the Government to identify the areas that 
are regularly affected by floods, as well as to devise measures 
that should be taken to control the fl oods. Only then, this 
problem can be solved. Calamities are taken very lightly and in 
a very casual manner. Whenever there are floods, people 
assess the situation through helicopters and so on and estimate 
the damages; and that's all. You have to solve the problem for 
all times to come. I do not think any long-term assistance has 
been given in this regard. I request the Government to lay a 
white paper on this issue. Also, we must have a foolproof flood 
management system and there s hould be a mechanism to 
control the floods. Many a time, floods are caused due to 
desiltation, deforestation and erosion of riverbanks. These are 
the main reasons for the floods. I would like to know whether the 
Government would come forward to save the life and property 
from the havoc caused by floods, especially in West Bengal, 
where the situation is alarming. So far as the State of West 
Bengal is concerned, there is also a report in which it is said that 
the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development informed that it was not in a position to provide any 
assistance because that Ministry does not administer any 
scheme which provides for repair of school buildings that have 
been damaged due to excessive rains and floods. 
201 

RAJYA  SABHA   [24 November, 2000] 
On the one hand, the houses and school buildings have 
been devastated; on the other, the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development is saying that it has no scheme for 
them, and it would not help. What type of attitude is this? 
Should this type of an attitude be adopted by the Government? 
I, therefore, request the Government that all efforts should be 
made to help these people. The farmers and villagers are 
affected the most by these floods. As compared to rural areas, 
urban areas are not affected much by these floods. So, the 70 
per cent of our population which is residing in villages is 
affected by these floods. These poor people are rendered 
homeless, landless and their crops are devastated by floods. 
The Government should see to it that some effective steps are 
taken in order to save these people from floods. The 
Government should formulate a long-term project so that the 
people are saved from these natural calamities. 
[The Vice-Chairman (Shri Suresh Pachouri) in the Chair.]

opportunity, Sir, to place my very sincere gratitude to all the hon. 
Members who participated and benefited me with their views. I 
am also, of course, very grateful to such hon. Members as have 
commended the work that the Ministry of External Affairs is 
doing; but, I remain equally, if not equally, only marginally less 
grateful to such Members as have found fault with us and 
suggested that we benefit by the views and advice that they had 
for us. Sir. you will appreciate that it will not be possible for me to 
take all the points that all the hon. Members had made. What I 
have done is to distil the common points that found echo in 
various hon. Members' participation in the debate, and from then, 
if there are any other additional points remaining, I will come to 
that.

very opening submissions to the House. Very befittingiy and

great personalities of the past, principally, to late Pandit

Members' point that a nostalgia for the past, or, about great

of the state of the world then existing, is a suitable approach to

statements were issued on several days. But from the very

immediately issued its viewpoint clearly and

was benefited by the views of Hon. Pranab Mukherjee and also 
a number of other hon. Members. There were mainly three

questioning the concept of minimum credible deterrent. The

asserting, simply on the basis of six or seven tests. The third

Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty. I cannot do Justice to this 
subject in its entirety, Mr. Vice-Chairman, because this is a 
subject by itself. No doubt, the Government will benefit, and I

deterrent, hon. Pranab Mukherjee, put across his viewpoint,

there existed a kind of ability and that was sufficient. I submit 
for the consideration of the House that that is a proposition or 
an advocacy of what I would call, concealed deterrence or 
possibly even technical deterrence, As against concealed 
deterrence or technical deterrent, the Government, after due 
and deliberate thought, took the decision to go in for a clear, 
credible, but a minimum deterrent. Minimum because, as I said 
in my opening remarks, that, in principle, culturally and 
civilizationally, India continues to belong to the world of 
disarmament and that is where, ultimately, it will have to go 
back. In the meantime, until the entire globe is rid of all its 
weapons of mass .destruction, we will have to continue to have 
a balance between the demands of real politic, the demands of 
national security and just and valid international concerns in

voluntarily put a moratorium on tests and we have also stated

Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, provided the international 
community arrived at a consensus in this regard, and provided, 
those that are covered under the relevant article of the 
Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, also adhere to it, without any 
additional pre-conditions or reservations.     The

That the Bill to provide for the prohibition of 
smoking of tobacco in any form in places of public 
work or use and in public service vehicles since 
smoking has been found injurious not only to the 
smokers but even more to the non-smokers and

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Madam, smoking 
considered as a private problem until yesterday is a public 
hazard today. It has been proved beyond any doubt that 
tobacco smoking is injurious not only for the one who indulges 
in it, but it is also as much, harmful, if not more, for those 
around. Cosmetic measures like advertising "Smoking is 
injurious for health" etc. may have succeeded to an extent in 
the developed countries but    these    have    registered    little    
impact    in    the    developing    and

underdeveloped countries. With the latest research revealing 
grave danger of passive smoking, it has become imperative to 
take stricter measures to curb this menace in our developing 
society in India. Hence this Bill about which the Government 
too, has already given an indication in reply to an Unstarred 
Question on December 10, 1999, that "the Government is 
examining the feasibility of formulating a comprehensive 
legislation for discouraging use of tobacco smoking." 
According to the Delhi Medical Association findings, 
recently reported in the Press, tobacco will emerge as a major 
killer by 2020.- It is estimated that nearly 3.5 million people 
annually die in the world from smoking-related diseases, of 
which two-thirds die in the developing countries. The World 
Health Organisation has reported that over 150 million children 
in the world die of tobacco-induced diseases, one-third of 
which, under five years, die due to acute respiratory infectious 
tobacco smoke. If the trend continues, tobacco use would kill 
nearly 10 million people every year. As it is, over 10 lakh 
people annually, or 3,000 every day, die on account of smoking 
in India. Several lakh more are disabled by tobacco-related 
diseases. The victims include those non-smokers who often 
remain in the company of smokers. 
The report goes on to say, "Tobacco contains harmful 
substances such as nicotine, carbon monoxide and lar. On 
inhalation, these substances enter the bloodstream affecting 
!he brain and causing heart and other ailments. Nicotine 
increases secretion of chemicals like adrenaline which 
increases the heart rate and blood pressure. Nicotine also 
interferes with the functioning of blood vessels, increasing the 
tendency of blood clots. Other adverse effects are respiratory 
infections, gastric ulcers, pregnancy complications, etc." 
Tobacco intake is a major contributing factor for 
causing cancer. It is reported that about 300 million would be 
afflicted by cancer in the next 25 years and about 200 million 
would die due to the disease. A WHO report says that tobacco 
use is responsible for 90 per cent of lung cancer and over 80 
per cent of chronic bronchitis cases. Also, 20 to 25 per cent of 
coronary heart diseases and stroke are attributed to smoking. 
Scientific data shows that there is unmistakable co-
relation between smoking and infertility. If a person smokes 
more than 20 cigarettes a day, his sperm count, a decisive 
factor in fertility, could drop by 60-70  per  cent.    The  infertility  
risk  is  not  confined  to men  alone.
